title: MacKenzie Scott gave Jeff Bezos 75% of their Amazon shares, Blue Origin, and the Washington Post in 2019 divorce
detail:
MacKenzie Scott gave Jeff Bezos 75% of their Amazon shares, Blue Origin, and the Washington Post in 2019 divorce
Kit Pulliam

When Jeff Bezos divorced MacKenzie Scott in 2019, the divorce was, at least outwardly, amicable.

"I'm grateful for [Scott's] support and for her kindness in this process and am very much looking forward to our new relationship as friends and co-parents," the then-55-year-old Bezos posted on X at the time.

Scott posted the same day.

"Grateful to have finished the process of dissolving my marriage with Jeff with support from each other," she wrote on X. "Looking forward to [the] next phase as co-parents and friends."

But there's no question that Bezos walked away with more equity. In the same post, Scott says she handed over all her interest in both the Washington Post and Blue Origin to Bezos.

She also allowed Bezos to take 75% of their joint Amazon stock, leaving her with just a four percent stake in the company compared to Bezos' 12%. As part of the deal, she also agreed to act as a proxy voter for Bezos, meaning she no longer had any voting rights on the stock she owned.

Here's some background on the deal — as well as how gender can impact divorce proceedings.

Washington's laws value equality between divorcing partners

Jeff Bezos and MacKenzie Scott lived in Seattle, Washington while they were married. Washington is a community property state, meaning that anything that a couple gains after marriage is a community good that belongs to both parties.

Bezos started Amazon in 1994, just one year after he and Scott were married. In fact, Bezos himself has talked about how important Scott was to his success with the company.

"MacKenzie, you know, she had married this stable guy working on Wall Street, and a year after we got married, I went to her and said I wanted to quit my job, move across the country, and start this internet bookstore," Bezos told Business Insider in 2018. "Even before she could say, 'What's the internet?' she said, 'Great — let's go!'"

His stock in Amazon is considered community property by Washington. Since Bezos founded Blue Origin in 2000 and bought the Washington Post in 2013, they also qualify.

During divorce proceedings, Washington state judges will attempt to make a "just and equitable distribution" of the divorcing couple's community property. This could mean splitting the property equally between the two, but it doesn't have to; judges are allowed to give one person 55% of the community property and another 45%, for instance.

title: Google to launch drone deliveries in UK
detail:
Google to launch drone deliveries in UK
Matthew Field
Sun, November 15, 2026 at 11:00 AM EST 2 min read
GOOGL
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
The service will be trialled across the West Midlands

Google is planning to launch drone deliveries to households in the UK for the first time in a challenge to Amazon's rival Prime Air service.

Wing, which is owned by the US search engine giant, is preparing to trial an airborne "last-mile delivery service" near Birmingham next year.

The drone company has already launched drone services in London, carrying blood samples for the NHS between hospitals in the capital.

However, its latest trial will deliver groceries and other household goods. If approved, Wing's new drone trials will be introduced in May and last up to three years.

Documents filed with the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) show Wing is targeting an area spanning Dudley, West Bromwich and Wolverhampton for its initial scheme.

A Wing spokesman said: "We are excited to explore expanding our service to more areas in the UK and extending our service to include a trial of residential drone delivery services.

"As an early step in that process, Wing has applied for an airspace change proposal with the CAA in the UK."

The trial, if approved, will allow Wing's four-bladed drones to "deliver groceries and everyday essentials to customers' doorsteps", the spokesman added.

It will also "provide valuable data to the CAA on operating in airspace alongside other airspace users, conducting multiple simultaneous operations, and routine automated beyond visual line of sight operations".

Wing already operates in multiple cities across the US, promising to deliver groceries in as little as 30 minutes. The company has a partnership with retail giant Walmart.

Its UK launch would put Wing into direct competition with Amazon, which has been expanding its own drone network in Britain.

Amazon launched its Prime Air service in May, serving around 600 homes around its Darlington warehouse. It has since expanded the scheme to cover around 8,000 households, delivering products weighing up to 2.2kg.

Drone deliveries have been slow to take off in the UK, with the CAA only approving limited trials that rely on bespoke airspace agreements.

It has been preparing to allow more widespread drone operations that will see aircraft fly beyond the horizon, sharing the sky with planes and other drones, with "routine" operations planned in 2027.

Previous drone trials by Wing in other markets have not always gone without a hitch.

In 2022, a Wing drone crashed into a power line in Australia, causing 2,000 households to lose power. In another incident, its operations were temporarily suspended after its drones were attacked by ravens.

Amazon was forced to suspend drone deliveries in 2025 after two of its aircraft crashed in the US.

Micron, Amazon, and IBM: My 3 Favorite Stocks to Buy and Hold Through 2030

Holding a stock through 2030 means keeping it for more than four years. A lot can go wrong with any one business in that time, so I'd rather not count on a single company for that long.

My three favorites today are Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), and International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM). They don't look like much of a group. Micron stock trades at under 5 times the earnings analysts expect for this fiscal year, while Amazon trades at around 25 times earnings, using analysts' 2027 forecasts. And IBM's dividend yields about 2.8%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But I think these differences are a big reason the three fit well together.

Image source: Micron.

1. Micron: The stock looks cheap for what it earns

Micron's growth in the last year has been stunning. Revenue more than tripled in fiscal 2026 to $133.2 billion (Micron's fiscal year ended Sept. 3, 2026), and net income climbed around tenfold to $85.0 billion.

The company's still growing, too. Revenue climbed to $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 from $41.5 billion the quarter before, and management expects about $61.5 billion in the current one -- slower sequential growth, but growth all the same.

Yet at roughly $820 as of this writing, shares cost under 5 times earnings, using analysts' forecasts for fiscal 2027. In other words, investors are arguably pricing in a steep fall in profits at some point.

There's history behind this doubt. In fiscal 2023, Micron's revenue was around half the prior year's, and the company lost $5.8 billion.

What makes me comfortable holding through 2030 is how much of the business is now under contract. Micron estimates that its 26 strategic customer agreements will make up over a third of its revenue through 2030. And most of that revenue comes with set pricing terms, often including floor and ceiling prices.

2. Amazon: AWS has years of work lined up

Amazon's cloud business is the top reason I'd hold the stock through 2030. Amazon Web Services (AWS) revenue climbed 39% year over year to $46.0 billion in the third quarter, its fastest growth in almost five years. And AWS brought in about 63% of Amazon's operating income on about 23% of its sales.

What's more, AWS's backlog (contracted revenue it hasn't recognized yet) hit $578 billion. That's over three years of revenue at AWS's current $184 billion annual run rate.

Investors who want to avoid Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) but put capital to work in growth-focused, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) face a difficult challenge. Nvidia is an integral part of index funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) -- as the second-largest S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) holding behind Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL). Nvidia also joined the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) in 2024. And Nvidia carries an especially high weighting in many growth ETFs and tech sector ETFs.

However, there is a unique low-cost Vanguard ETF that doesn't own Nvidia yet still holds Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Apple, and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) as its top three holdings.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

A value ETF for the modern market

The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF (NASDAQ:VONV) is a modern take on value stocks. While the Vanguard Growth ETF, Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF, and Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF label most major tech-focused companies as growth stocks, the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF takes a nuanced approach.

The Russell 1000 is the 1,000 largest U.S. listed companies by market cap. It includes smaller large-cap and mid-cap stocks, whereas the S&P 500 just has large-cap stocks.

FTSE Russell, a subsidiary of the London Stock Exchange Group, has a semi-annual reconstitution whereby it roughly splits the market cap weighting of the Russell 1000 into two indexes -- the Russell 1000 Value Index (which the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF tracks) and the Russell 1000 Growth Index -- which is mirrored by the Vanguard Russell 1000 Growth ETF. If FTSE Russell categorized all tech-focused companies as growth stocks, then the growth index would have a far higher market cap than the value index. So instead, FTSE Russell categorizes some established companies that were formerly high-octane growth stocks as value stocks, like Amazon, which is in the value index and not the growth index. Some stocks have their market caps split between both indexes. For example, Apple and Microsoft are top holdings in both indexes, whereas Nvidia, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta Platforms, and Tesla -- among other names -- are solely in the growth index.

As a result, the Russell 1000 Value ETF's three largest holdings are Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft -- which make up a combined 17.4% of the ETF as of Sept. 30. Normally, Apple and Microsoft would have higher weightings than Amazon because they have higher market caps. But since all of Amazon's market cap is weighted exclusively by the value index while Apple and Microsoft are split, Amazon is actually the largest individual holding in the Russell 1000 Value ETF.

Key Takeaways

Qualcomm's handset revenue fell 26% to $5.14 billion, missing estimates, while automotive revenue jumped 89% to a record $1.99 billion.

CEO Cristiano Amon told Reuters that non-handset growth should "replace Apple entirely," with fiscal 2027 guidance assuming no more Apple chip sales.

Rising costs cut the chip segment's pretax margin to 24% from 29%, and Bernstein called the margin outlook "lousy."

Qualcomm's next report should show whether data center revenue tops $650 million and whether price increases start lifting margins.

Qualcomm (QCOM:NASDAQ) just posted a quarter that showed both of its futures at once. Phone chip sales shrank by more than a quarter, while car chip sales nearly doubled.

Investors focused on the phones. Shares fell more than 6% in extended trading on November 4 after handset revenue missed estimates, partly because Apple (AAPL:NASDAQ) keeps moving to its own modems.

The offsets are getting bigger, though. Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) can buy up to $60 billion of Qualcomm's AI data center chips under a September deal. On earnings day, SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) also picked Qualcomm to supply radio gear for its planned Starlink Mobile network starting in 2027.

In an interview with Reuters, CEO Cristiano Amon said the first-quarter forecast includes no further Apple sales. "We expect the non-handset (revenue) to replace Apple entirely," he said.

Phones fell while cars surged

Adjusted revenue fell 7% to $10.44 billion, beating the $10.11 billion analysts expected. Adjusted EPS came in at $2.17, a penny above estimates but down 28% from a year earlier.

The split inside the chip business told the real story:

Handsets: $5.14 billion, down 26% and below the $5.25 billion estimate

Automotive: $1.99 billion, up 89% for a first $2 billion quarter

IoT: $1.89 billion, up 4%

Memory explains most of the damage. Surging memory costs pushed up phone prices, and global smartphone shipments fell 20% in the quarter to a 14-year low. Qualcomm's handset drop was steeper still because Apple orders are fading.

Here's how fast the mix is moving…

Qualcomm (QCOM): QCT revenue by segment, $ billions, fiscal 2021–2026 (TIKR)

In fiscal 2026, automotive and IoT made up about 35% of chip revenue, up from roughly 28% a year earlier.

Data center becomes the swing factor

Fiscal 2027 is where the plan gets tested. Qualcomm expects more than $650 million of data center revenue in the December quarter, ahead of the $539 million analysts had penciled in. It reiterated a $5 billion full-year target.

Amazon anchors that ramp. Qualcomm supplies custom inference silicon and optical connectivity to AWS, and Amazon's warrants for up to 25 million Qualcomm shares vest as it buys.

Amazon.com runs a global online and physical retail operation and sells advertising and subscription services, with warehouse labor forming a core part of how it fulfills orders. That makes union outcomes in Canada relevant for how you think about the firm's broader cost structure and workforce practices across its logistics network.

4 things going right for Amazon.com that this headline doesn't cover.

What Amazon's first union contract really tests in its AI and infrastructure Narrative

Amazon.com's Narrative asks you to back a business pouring huge sums into AI, data centers and satellites on the assumption that high-margin AWS, ads and long-duration contracts more than earn that spend. A binding union deal in a core warehouse hints at how labor terms might reshape the cost base supporting that bet.

"The main thing that has to go right is that Amazon.com turns its very large AI focused CapEx program, including data centers, servers and satellite infrastructure, into long duration contracts that sustain strong free cash flow and attractive returns on invested capital..."

See how the full story points towards a $331 fair value for Amazon.com.

The Canadian contract quietly backs part of the bull case. It shows regulators and unions converting pressure into defined rules rather than open-ended friction, which can give investors clearer lines around warehouse wages and protections while Amazon leans on automation and AI-led routing to keep logistics productivity improving in the background.

The bear side is that each successful organizing effort can set a reference point for workers elsewhere, including in the US, pulling more of Amazon.com's fulfillment network into formal bargaining and making it harder to offset higher pay with efficiency gains alone. For comparison, Walmart and Target have kept unions at the edges of their US operations, so an Amazon network with more formalized labor could carry structurally different fixed costs.

Alphabet has two share classes that trade publicly. Class A shares (GOOGL) carry voting rights. Alphabet Class C (NASDAQ:GOOG) has none. Class B is held by insiders and does not trade publicly. The S&P 500 weights stocks by market value, and it gives each public class its own position.
